title: The Open vSwitch Database Management Protocol
summary: Defines the OVSDB management protocol for Open vSwitch, an open-source virtual switch for virtualized servers that forwards traffic between virtual machines and the physical network. Open vSwitch can also be controlled with OpenFlow, and OVSDB is used to manage it. Open-source client and server implementations exist.

plainLanguage.summary: A virtual switch is a pretend network box inside a computer. This is how you talk to it to set it up.

questions: how to configure open vswitch remotely
subtitle: A JSON-RPC protocol for remotely managing Open vSwitch virtual switches in data centers.

tldr.problem: Open vSwitch is widely used as a virtual switch in virtualized server environments, but it needed a standard way for management systems to configure and monitor it remotely.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7047 defines the OVSDB protocol, which uses JSON-RPC 1.0 over TCP to provide database operations (insert, select, update, delete) against an internal configuration database, plus transaction support, change monitoring, and locking.
tldr.outcome: OVSDB enables centralized management of virtual networking in cloud and virtualization platforms. Open vSwitch includes open-source OVSDB server and client implementations.

facts.label: Key database operations
facts.value: insert, select, update, mutate, delete, wait, commit

today: RFC 7047 remains an Informational RFC. OVSDB is widely deployed as the configuration management protocol for Open vSwitch, which is extensively used in cloud platforms (like OpenStack) and virtualized data centers for software-defined networking. The RFC documents the protocol used by the open-source Open vSwitch project.

sections.title: Configuring Virtual Switches
sections.content:
Open vSwitch (OVS) is an open-source software switch used in virtualized server environments. It forwards traffic between virtual machines (VMs) on the same physical host and between VMs and the physical network. The RFC defines OVSDB, the protocol for managing and configuring Open vSwitch instances remotely.

An OVS instance consists of a database server (ovsdb-server), a switch daemon (ovs-vswitchd), and optionally a fast-path forwarding module. Management systems connect via OVSDB to perform configuration; controllers connect via OpenFlow (a separate protocol) to manage traffic forwarding. OVSDB handles slow operations like creating bridges and ports; OpenFlow handles fast packet forwarding decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Open vSwitch has a database server that knows the switch's configuration. OVSDB is how you talk to that server from a management computer to set things up.

sections.title: Architecture and Management Operations
sections.content:
OVSDB allows managers to perform a wide range of operations on an Open vSwitch instance:

Datapath management: Create, modify, and delete OpenFlow datapaths (bridges), and configure which controllers they connect to. Port and interface management: Create, modify, and delete ports and tunnel interfaces on bridges. Quality of Service: Create and manage queues, and attach QoS policies to ports. Statistics: Query performance and traffic statistics. Manager configuration: Configure which management systems can connect to the OVSDB server.

Importantly, OVSDB does not perform per-flow operations: that is left to OpenFlow. OVSDB is for configuration and monitoring at a much longer timescale than packet forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: OVSDB lets you add ports, create virtual bridges, set up tunnels, define quality-of-service rules, and see statistics. The actual sending of packets is handled by a different protocol called OpenFlow.

sections.title: Wire Protocol and RPC Methods
sections.content:
OVSDB uses JSON-RPC 1.0 as its wire protocol, implemented over TCP. Clients send JSON-RPC requests and receive responses. The protocol defines several RPC methods:

list_dbs: Lists the names of databases available on the server. get_schema: Retrieves the schema of a database, describing its tables, columns, and constraints. transact: Executes a series of database operations as a single atomic transaction. This is the main method for all read and write operations. monitor/monitor_cancel: Subscribe to changes in a table and receive notifications of inserts, deletes, and modifications. lock/steal/unlock: Acquire and release locks on the database for coordinating multiple clients. echo: A liveness check, echoing back its parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends commands in JSON format. It can ask for a list of databases, get the schema, run transactions, watch for changes, or grab locks to prevent conflicts.

sections.title: Database Operations
sections.content:
The heart of OVSDB is the transact method, which accepts a series of database operations to be executed atomically. Each operation is a JSON object describing what to do:

insert: Add a new row to a table. The server assigns it a unique UUID. select: Query rows from a table using conditions. update: Modify specific columns in rows matching conditions. mutate: Apply mathematical operations (arithmetic, set insertion/deletion) to columns in matching rows. delete: Remove rows matching conditions. wait: Block the transaction until a condition becomes true or timeout expires. commit: Mark the transaction as durable (written to disk). abort: Roll back the transaction.

All operations in a transaction are atomic: they either all succeed or all fail together. The database enforces constraints like referential integrity and uniqueness indexes at commit time.
sections.plainLanguage: A transaction is like a recipe with steps. You can insert rows, find rows, change them, delete them, or wait for something to happen. Either all steps work or none of them do.

sections.title: Database Structure and Change Monitoring
sections.content:
An OVSDB database consists of tables, each with rows and columns. Every row has two special columns: _uuid, a unique identifier that never changes, and _version, a version number that changes whenever the row is modified. _version is ephemeral: it changes each time the database restarts.

The database schema is itself a JSON structure that describes table names, column types (integer, real, boolean, string, UUID), constraints (min/max, enum values, referential integrity), and metadata. Clients can retrieve the schema using the get_schema method to discover what tables and operations are available.

The monitor method allows clients to subscribe to a table and receive change notifications. Clients specify which columns to monitor and which types of changes to receive (initial rows, inserts, deletes, modifications). The server automatically sends update notifications whenever the monitored table changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every row has a unique ID and a version number that increments when it changes. Clients can ask the server to watch a table and get notified whenever something changes.
